# The Scoop source code reconstruction using LLMs

This is a work in progress project to reconstruct the source code for the MS-DOS version of the Microprose game ["The Scoop"](https://www.mobygames.com/game/4795/the-scoop/). The original game was written in C. The C source code was compiled with the Microsoft C compiler v5.0 and it uses the [compact memory model](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/X86_memory_models).

The reconstruction aims to be bug-for-bug faithful, and the C routines yield code that's identical to the original at the CPU instruction level (when compiled with the same compiler with appropriate flags), while allowing for layout differences in the executables.

This is just the reconstruction project; porting to a modern OS, potential improvements and bugfixes will be targeted by a separate project in the future.

This repository contains no game assets, executables or other copyrighted material, it's a clean rewrite of the game's source code based on the analysis of the game binaries obtained from the original floppy disks, for preservation and historical research purposes, and as such should fall under the interoperability exemption of the DMCA.

The general idea of doing a source code reconstruction and most of the scripts were based on [the excelent F-15 Strike Eagle 2 reconstruction](https://github.com/neuviemeporte/f15se2-re). Very recommended to take a look there if you want to see a professional (and advanced!) reconstruction project.

The main difference betweeh the f15se2-re project and this reconstruction is the experimentation using LLMs to iterate on the C code until to make the process scalable.

# Executable

The game executable is compressed using EXEPack. The sha256 signatures are:

* `34f8a654a3c46095d48dcc76ecf088cb90655972794b8ecb4d87927f5a295b9b  game/SCOOP.EXE`
* `343320c1a103729df3d69bebf887f1c5d3c9bf38890ff3ec6ec4d515c40d9b5b  game/SCOOP.EXE` (unpacked using [unEXEPack](https://github.com/w4kfu/unEXEPACK))

# Status

As of the time of writing this, the reconstruction has not started yet. We are just testing the technology to see if it works and setting up the initial scripts to automatically compile the complete binary and compare it with the original one. It is unclear if the technology is good enough, but some results are promising. Check the [src/recovered folder](https://github.com/neuromancer/the-scoop-re/tree/main/src/recovered) to see examples of reconstructed functions. All the reconstructored source code was producing using [Gemini 2.5](https://blog.google/technology/google-deepmind/gemini-model-thinking-updates-march-2025/).

# Building

Prerequisites:

* a copy of the MS C v5.0 compiler placed in the `dos/msc5` directory
* the `dosbox` emulator has been installed
* relatively recent (3.8-ish) Python installed

Instructions are WIP, but the idea is to clone the project and run `make` inside. It will download and build the `mzretools` and `UASM` repositories as part of the build process. The build process is not complete yet and it is still a copy of the f15se2-re one.

# Verification

The Makefile contains a target for automatically comparing the reconstruction with the original using the `mzdiff` tool but the verification is not ready to work.

bkarak-pharaoh-xxxv-readme-md.text:
# The Anger of Pharaoh XXXV — browser re-creation

A faithful HTML re-implementation of the 1997 DOS text-parser adventure. The original engine
(`GAME.EXE`, Borland C++) was reverse-engineered from the binary; the game's own data files are
extracted at build time and the JavaScript engine reproduces the interpreter, parser, VGA console,
menus, palette fades and PC-speaker beeps. Nothing about the game was rewritten by hand: rooms,
sprites, texts, puzzles and the spirit's dialogue tree all come from `GAME.DAT`.

The reverse-engineering and the re-implementation were done by Claude Code (Anthropic's coding
agent) on 2026-09-02, from the binary and the data files alone, directed by Vassilios Karakoidas,
one of the game's two authors.

Play it at [bkarak.wizhut.tech/software/pharaoh](https://bkarak.wizhut.tech/software/pharaoh).
The story of the reverse-engineering is in [REVERSE-ENGINEERING.md](REVERSE-ENGINEERING.md)
and the recovered file formats in [FORMAT.md](FORMAT.md).

## Layout

```
original/   the DOS files (GAME.EXE, GAME.DAT, CHAR.DAT, BEGIN/END/END1-5.GFX) — not in the repo, see below
tools/extract.py   GAME.DAT + friends -> dist/assets.json (+ deflated base64 copy)
tools/build.py     extract, then inline engine + data into dist/pharaoh.html (+ dist/pharaoh-embed.html)
tools/re/          the throwaway analysis scripts, in the order they were used
src/engine.js      the engine (one routine per original function, offsets in comments)
dist/pharaoh.html  the single-file deliverable (build output, not committed)
FORMAT.md          the reverse-engineered file formats and script semantics
```

The original game files are not part of this repository. They are the 1997 freeware release,
[game.zip](https://bkarak.wizhut.tech/programs/game/game.zip) (10 files, 668 KB); unzip it into
`original/` — the names are already lower-case, which is what the extractor expects.

## Build

```bash
python3 tools/build.py
```

Then open `dist/pharaoh.html` (any static server, or `python3 -m http.server --directory dist`).
The page needs `DecompressionStream`, available in every current browser. Python 3 with nothing
installed is enough; only the analysis scripts under `tools/re/` want Capstone and Pillow.

The build also writes `dist/pharaoh-embed.html`, the bare screen with no chrome, meant for an
`<iframe>` on another page. `--site DIR` copies the two into `DIR` as `index.html` and
`embed.html`; that is how the game is published on the site above.

`Pharaoh.debug()` exposes `present`, the framebuffer-to-canvas paint, so a script can capture
the screen from a background tab where `requestAnimationFrame` never fires; `Pharaoh.pushKey`
feeds the key queue for the same purpose.

## Walkthrough (spoilers)

1. Dark room: `TAKE EYE`, `USE EYE WITH PAINTING`, `GO NORTH`.
2. Corridor: `TAKE THING IN THE WATER`, `EXAMINE THING IN THE WATER` (three rocks), `GO AHEAD`.
3. Coffin room: `USE RED ROCK WITH LEFT TRIANGLE`, `USE BLUE ROCK WITH RIGHT TRIANGLE`,
   `USE GREEN ROCK WITH UPPER TRIANGLE`, then `TAKE MUMMY`, `GO DOWN`.
4. Hidden room: `USE BUTTON` (or `GO NORTH`) — you get trapped, but both doors upstairs open.
   `GO SOUTH`, `GO EAST`.
5. Pharaoh room: `TAKE VASE`, `USE SAND WITH VASE`, `USE VASE WITH SAND WITH PILLAR`, `TAKE ROCK`,
   `GO SOUTH`, `GO NORTH`.
6. Last room: `USE ROCK WITH SOCKET`, then answer 2, 1, 1, 2. Every other branch kills you.

## Differences from the DOS version

- Quitting returns to the title screen instead of DOS.
- Palette fades run at a fixed 14 ms per step instead of the monitor's vertical retrace.
- The random number source is `Math.random()` rather than the PIT timer.

btpf-re-payback-readme-md.text:
# Payback reimplementation

A reverse-engineered reimplementation of [Payback](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Payback_(video_game)) (Apex Designs, Amiga, 2001) in Rust with [Bevy](https://bevyengine.org), plus the research behind it.

If there are any issues, please open an issue or PR with screenshot preferably and I would happily review the changes. 

![](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1c722d22-5d59-4d39-82ff-dae729981208)
### Features

- A from-scratch Rust and Bevy reimplementation of *Payback* (Apex Designs, 2001), built from reverse-engineering the original Amiga and Mac releases.
- Game logic follows the decompiled originals function by function: driving physics, collisions, AI traffic and police, pedestrians, combat, the wanted level and scoring. Code comments cite the original function and address.
- A toggle to switch between Amiga Assets and MacOS Release Assets
  - Both Intro videos
  - Both Textures
  - Both Models
- Quality Of Life Improvements
  - Smooth Motion Interpolation to any frame rate
  - A custom Cheat menu by pressing F12
  - Modern Controller Support
  - Ability to unlock all straight from the main menu

### Motivations

Payback was a GTA Clone for the Commodore Amiga and PPC Mac Computers. It was a childhood favorite of mine but as of 2026 is impossible to emulate at full speed and quality, and difficult to play without the original vintage hardware. 

I created this in the name of preservation and to test the reverse engineering capabilities of frontier AI Models.
The bulk of this game was recreated in ~3 days using opus 5.5 at medium effort and used around \$1500 worth of API Credits.

I had no prior knowledge of the original Motorola 68k Instruction Set, nor any ability to reverse engineer. This was all done with a handful of short high level prompts and some manual testing.

## Quick Start Instructions

In order to play, either the MacOS or the amiga version are needed.

Providing both version will allow you to toggle between the platform specific features in game.

```
payback.exe
payback-extract.exe
Payback Game + Updates\
    Amiga\
        - the Amiga CD (.zip, .bin, .cue, .iso)
        - PaybackUpdate7.lha
    MacOS\
        - PaybackMac.toast
```
When you run `payback-extract.exe`, all of the necessary game files will be extracted.

Music will also be extracted from the Amiga CD files if they are present.

Required File Downloads:
- `PaybackMac.toast` - Can be found here: https://www.myabandonware.com/game/payback-3of#download
- `Payback (Europe).zip` - https://archive.org/download/commodore_amiga_cd/Payback%20%28Europe%29.zip
- `PaybackUpdate7.lha` - https://www.apex-designs.net/payback_update_amiga.html



## AI Written & Maintained Notes Below

It is a **behavioural port**, not a matching decompilation: the game logic is
rewritten from the decompiled original (the Amiga Update 7 and AmigaOS 4 builds
and the later Mac OS release, whose OS X build kept its function names) and
checked against it function by function. The Mac release is treated as the
definitive version; where the Amiga version differs, a setting picks it.

**Status:** playable end to end. The six story levels, Rampage (with the Mac's
random phone missions), 2-4 player split screen, replays, saves, the front end,
HUD, sound and the Mac intro film are in, with software and hardware (Warp3D-style)
renderers and a WebAssembly build. Details and what is left:
[`docs/status.md`](docs/status.md).

## Legal

No original game data and no decompiled code are in this repository, and none
may be committed: you need your own copy of the game. Everything derived from it
(`extracted/`, `analysis/`, `out/`, `web/dist/`, the report pages) is git-ignored.
The notes in `docs/` describe the original's behaviour in their own words and
quote at most a few lines (see [`docs/CONVENTIONS.md`](docs/CONVENTIONS.md)).

## Playing

You need your own copy of the game: the Amiga CD (with Update 7), the Mac
CD, or both. Next to `payback.exe` (a release build: `target/release/`, or a
copy of that folder) is an empty folder `Payback Game + Updates/`. Put your
files in it:

| Folder | Files |
|---|---|
| `Amiga/` | the Amiga CD: `.iso`, `.cue` with its `.bin` file(s) (one for the disc or one per track), or a `.zip` / `.rar` holding them; and `PaybackUpdate7.lha` next to it (the OS4 port and Warp3D archives are not needed) |
| `MacOS/` | `PaybackMac.toast` |

Then run `payback-extract.exe` from the same folder. It lists what it
found and asks: press Enter to extract (or re-extract, replacing what was
extracted before), or type `q` and Enter to close without changing
anything. It writes the files the game reads into `data/amiga` and
`data/mac`, and the CD's music tracks into `Music/` as FLAC (from a
`.bin`/`.cue` image; an `.iso` has no audio). `--list` only lists, `--yes`
skips the question. Start `payback.exe`; without extracted data it says
what to do and closes.
(`crates/payback-extract`; it needs no other software.)

## Quick start (from source)

**Prerequisites:** Rust (edition 2024, stable); Python 3.11+ with `7z` on the
`PATH` (and `pip install machfs` for the Mac release); for the RE tools also
`pip install capstone numpy pillow markdown`; Docker for the decompiles; for the
web build see [`docs/web.md`](docs/web.md).

1. **Get the data.** Put your copies in `Payback Game + Updates/` in the
   repository: `Amiga/Payback.iso`,
   `Amiga/Updates/PaybackUpdate7.lha` (and optionally
   `Amiga/Updates/paybackupdateOS4Native.lha`, `Amiga/Updates/Warp3D-42.lha`,
   and the Mac release `MacOS/PaybackMac.toast`). Then unpack them for the
   build and the RE tools:

   ```sh
   python tools/extract/extract.py       # -> extracted/game (CD + Update 7), iso, os4, ...
   python tools/extract/extract_mac.py   # -> extracted/mac (optional, recommended)
   ```

   Either release alone also works: with only `PaybackMac.toast` the game
   runs from the Mac data (Mac content; English, Deutsch and Français; no
   Amiga variants, FLC intro or shipped replays). `--mac-only` tries that
   setup while the Amiga data is present.

2. **Build and run.**

   ```sh
   cargo run --release -p payback                  # menus
   cargo run --release -p payback -- --map 0       # straight into city 0, level 0
   ```

   The build copies the data files the game reads next to the executable
   (`target/<profile>/data/amiga` and `data/mac`, hard links where it can;
   the list is [`crates/payback/data_files.txt`](crates/payback/data_files.txt)),
   so `target/release/` is a self-contained folder: double-click
   `payback.exe`, or copy the folder elsewhere and run it there. It also
   creates the empty `Payback Game + Updates/Amiga` and `MacOS` folders
   there for `payback-extract` (`cargo build --release` builds
   both executables). The data is your own copy of the game: never commit
   or share it.

   Where the game looks for its data, first match wins: `PAYBACK_DATA` /
   `PAYBACK_MAC_DATA`, `--data <dir>` / `--mac-data <dir>`; `data/amiga` and
   `data/mac` next to the executable; the folders named in
   `payback-data.cfg` next to the executable (`game = <dir>`, `mac = <dir>`); `extracted/game` and
   `extracted/mac/Payback` in the executable's folder or any folder above it,
   then in the working directory or above. If neither is found, a message
   box says the game files must be extracted (see "Playing") and the game
   closes. The log says which folders were used. `PAYBACK_NO_DIALOG=1`
   turns the message boxes off (headless runs). `PAYBACK_STAGE_DATA=0` builds without
   staging the data (`=copy` copies instead of linking);
   `python tools/dist/stage_data.py <dir>` stages it next to an executable
   elsewhere.

   `--screenshot out.png` saves a frame and exits; the
   full option list is at the top of `crates/payback/src/main.rs`, the controls
   in [`docs/controls.md`](docs/controls.md).

3. **Web build** (optional): `tools/web/build_web.sh`, then serve `web/dist/`
   ([`docs/web.md`](docs/web.md)).

## Custom maps

Community maps (e.g. from <https://www.apex-designs.net/payback_maps/>) work
as the Apex site describes: unzip the map and copy its files
(`<name>.map`, `.route`, `.vehicles`, `.mini`, `.thumb`, and `.textures` /
`.scores` when present; not the `__MACOSX` folder) into a `UserMaps/` folder
next to `payback.exe`. The map is then offered after the three cities in
Rampage and multiplayer. A map installed there replaces a bundled one of the
same name (the Mac release ships 31 community maps).

## Music

The game's music is the Red Book audio on the game CD; `Payback.iso` and
`PaybackMac.toast` hold only data. `payback-extract` takes it from a
`.bin`/`.cue` image of the CD (see "Playing"). Or rip the audio tracks from
your CD (any of WAV, Ogg Vorbis, MP3, FLAC) into a `Music/` folder next to `payback.exe` (beside `UserMaps/` and
`Saves/`; in a source checkout, `target/release/Music/`), one file per track,
named by its CD track number: `13.ogg`, `13 - anything.flac` or
`Track13.wav`. Track 1 is the data track: rip tracks 2–16. Without
tracks the Music setup shows the mode as Disabled.

Music and sound have separate volume sliders: "Music volume" on the
Music setup screen, and the Sound and Music bars in the pause menu (fire
switches bars, up/down change the selected one). (On the Mac the music
followed the sound volume and went silent with the sound at 100.)

From a raw BIN/CUE image of the CD (2352-byte sectors; one `.bin` for the
disc or one per track, as in the Redump set), or a `.zip` holding one,
`python tools/extract/rip_cd_tracks.py <cue or zip> <Music dir> [--flac]`
also splits the tracks out (defaults: the first `.cue`, else `.zip`, in
`Payback Game + Updates/Amiga/`, into `target/release/Music`; `--flac` needs
`ffmpeg`).

| CD track | Plays |
|---|---|
| 2 | radio: Limo, Hotrod |
| 3 | radio: Taxi |
| 4 | radio: Vapour |
| 5 | radio: Diblo, Pug Racer, Vapour GT |
| 6 | radio: Pug GTI |
| 7 | radio: Mundaneo, Fjord |
| 8 | Level / Game Complete; radio: Boat |
| 9 | radio: Evo |
| 10 | radio: Scooby |
| 11 | radio: Pug |
| 12 | radio: Truck, Rocket car |
| 13 | all menus |
| 14 | radio: Pickup truck |
| 15 | radio: Van |
| 16 | Game Over; radio: RC truck, Remote controlled car |

Bus, police vehicles, Tank, Ice cream van and Helicopter have no radio. In
Continuous mode every track plays in number order. The release names no
track titles (the credits list the artists only); details in
[`docs/re/frontend_audio.md`](docs/re/frontend_audio.md) §4.6.

## Verify

```sh
cargo test -p payback -p payback-formats             # data tests run when extracted/ exists
python tools/checks/replay_check.py --suite          # replay determinism: every case must MATCH
tools/checks/autoplay_all.sh                         # the bot plays the six story levels
```

The replay suite records a scripted run and plays it back with the same build;
it checks that the port is deterministic, not that it matches the original.
`tools/checks/` also has a frame-time check, a user-map smoke test and a
headless-browser test for the web build ([`tools/README.md`](tools/README.md)).

## Reverse engineering

```sh
docker build -t payback-re .         # Ghidra 12.1.4 workbench
tools/ghidra/decompile_all.sh        # fills analysis/ with every decompile
python tools/re/fn.py macx DrawMap   # print a function; --sym translates between builds
```

Then read [`docs/README.md`](docs/README.md), the index of the notes, and
[`docs/decompiling.md`](docs/decompiling.md).

## Layout

| Path | Contents |
|---|---|
| `crates/payback-formats/` | engine-independent parsers for the game's files |
| `crates/payback/` | the Bevy game |
| `crates/payback-mpeg/` | MPEG-1 playback for the Mac intro film (vendored `pl_mpeg`, MIT) |
| `docs/` | RE notes and project docs ([index](docs/README.md)) |
| `tools/` | extraction, Ghidra, RE helpers, checks, reports, web build ([index](tools/README.md)) |
| `web/` | the WebAssembly loader page |
| `Dockerfile` | RE workbench: Ghidra, radare2, amitools, FS-UAE, Rust |
| `target/<profile>/data/` | git-ignored: the game data staged next to the built executable |
| `extracted/`, `analysis/`, `out/`, `scratch/` | git-ignored: your game data, the decompiles, generated output, throwaway work |

## Contributing

See [`CONTRIBUTING.md`](CONTRIBUTING.md).

colbyshores-linewarsii-dos-readme-md.text:
# LineWars II, reconstructed

LineWars II is a 1994 DOS space-combat game by Patrick Aalto, published by Safari
Software. This is its engine, rebuilt in C from the shipped binary. It builds to
a single `game.exe` (107,200 bytes) that plays all ten missions in DOSBox-X:
cockpit, HUD, radar, scanner, sound, music, the config screen, the attract-mode
demo.

![Title screen](docs/captures/title.png)
![The demo mission: Cobra fighters attacking a defended StarBase](docs/captures/flight.png)

## Just want to play it

`dist/` is a prebuilt, ready-to-run package: no compiler, no build step. It has
`GAME.EXE` and `GAME.DAT`, a bootable FreeDOS hard-disk image
(`LINEWARS2-HD.img`, what `Play.bat` boots; built by `tools/make_hd_image.sh`),
the same thing as a bootable floppy (`LINEWARS2.img`), a `Play.bat` launcher,
and a `README.txt`. Install DOSBox-X (free, dosbox-x.org), double-click
`Play.bat`, and it boots straight into the game. It runs from wherever you unzip it. The rest of this document is for
building from source.

## Provenance and permission

LineWars II is © 1994 Patrick Aalto. I contacted him before releasing anything,
and he gave the project his blessing in July 2026: the reconstruction may be
released as freeware in any form; any commercial use requires a separate
licensing discussion with him. This repo stays on the freeware side of that
line. `NOTICE.md` has the full terms.

## What this is, and isn't

This is a behavioral reconstruction of the retail binary, not a matching
decompilation. The C builds with Open Watcom, so the compiled opcodes
deliberately don't match the original executable. The goal was portable C that
computes & draws what the 1994 game computes & draws, verified mechanically
rather than by eyeball.

The verification suite is 41 automated gates; 27 of them execute the original
machine code under emulation and diff it against this build: function return
values over swept input domains (`lw2_atan_base` alone is checked on all 78,060
golden vectors), VGA port writes, all ten mission spawn tables byte-for-byte,
and a frozen scene compared across all 153,600 framebuffer bytes. When the C
drifts from the original, the build goes red.

What's gate-proven versus what's merely implemented:

| Area | Status |
| --- | --- |
| VGA rendering, fixed-point math, game logic, all 10 mission spawn tables | Gate-proven against the original's executing bytes |
| Audio (PC speaker via the `SPEAKER.LW2` driver; Sound Blaster DSP/DMA and its music driver), keyboard | Implemented and play-tested; not oracle-gated |
| Serial/modem multiplayer modes (Duel/Wing/Group/StarWars) | Stubbed behind a notice screen; the original expects a serial peer |
| The original's other sound devices (Covox 8-bit DAC, Gravis UltraSound, Roland LAPC-I, Roland SCC-1) and video drivers (S3, VESA, ATI, MCGA) | Not scoped; VGA plus the two audio paths above are what this build supports |

If you find behavior that diverges from the original inside the gated envelope,
that's a bug. File it.

Every function reconstructed from the original carries the offset it came from.
`/* @0x24a4..0x24a7 */` in `lw2_flight.c` means those four bytes of the original
image are what that line reconstructs. That's deliberate: it's how a bug found
in 2030 gets traced back to the 1994 code. (A separate SDL3 port,
<https://github.com/fredangstadt-lang/LineWarsII-SDL>, strips all of it, since
a port needs the behaviour, not the provenance.)

## How it was made

LLM agents wrote it: Claude Opus 4.8 & Fable 5 leading, smaller models as
workers, one operator driving. 12 calendar days in July 2026, 10 of them
active, $2,655.98 in API tokens across 12,310 calls. Those figures are parsed
from the run's own transcripts. I'm not going to spend effort proving the
timeline; believe it or don't. The artifact is the part I'll defend.

It was not a straight line. Week one produced exactly what the literature
predicts from LLM decompilation: plausible, confident, fabricated code. At one
point a subagent reported MISSION WON on a build that crashed at launch. It was
caught the old way, by a human playing the game. The response was mechanical:
every prior claim was re-audited against freshly-run disassembly, and from July
3 onward no change shipped without a gate executing the original's bytes voting
on it. Two of the uglier finds along the way: a silent DGROUP exhaustion that
starved getenv() and killed all sound, and an optimizer dropping the segment
half of a far pointer.

## Where development happens

This repository is the archive: the disassembly annotations, the gates, and the
DOS build, kept intact as the reference for whatever needs digging up later.
New features do not land here. Future work (TCP/IP multiplayer, missile use by
enemy and friendly AI as a settings toggle, a customizable 10th mission, further
ports) happens in the SDL repo:
<https://github.com/fredangstadt-lang/LineWarsII-SDL>.

## What's here

```
engine/       23 C modules and their headers. 20 are linked into game.exe;
              lw2_setup.c, lw2_object.c and lw2_image.c are earlier
              reconstructions kept for reference and for the tests.
tests/        41 gates. unit/ = golden-vector tests; oracle/ = the Unicorn
              harness that executes the original bytes; stubs/ = link stubs.
tools/        build scripts, the codegen gate, the naming and style checkers,
              the performance bench, generators/ for the extracted-data headers.
reference/    the original game and the dumps every gate diffs against.
docs/         the reverse-engineering log, per-module notes for 9 of the
              modules under docs/engine/, and screenshots in docs/captures/.
data/         game.dat, the assets the engine reads at runtime.
```

## Prerequisites

None of these is vendored here; all are free.

- **Open Watcom 2.0** to build the DOS binary (<https://open-watcom.github.io>).
  Point `WATCOM` at your install, or drop one in `tools/watcom/ow2`:
  ```
  $env:WATCOM = "C:\WATCOM"        # PowerShell
  export WATCOM=/opt/watcom        # bash
  ```
- **gcc** and **bash** to build and drive the tests.
- **Python 3**, with **`unicorn`** (`pip install unicorn`) for the oracle gates.
  Without unicorn, 27 of the 41 gates can't run, and the suite fails rather than
  reporting success on the 14 that remain. Without Python at all, the suite fails
  outright.

## Build

```
powershell -File tools\build_game.ps1
```
Tested with Windows PowerShell 5.1 and Open Watcom 2.0 beta. Writes
`engine/game.exe`, 107,200 bytes. To play it, put `game.exe` and `data/game.dat`
in one directory and point DOSBox-X at it.

The build is deliberately split. Everything an interrupt can reach compiles `-2`,
because the 16-bit ISR prologue doesn't preserve the upper halves of 32-bit
registers, and a full `-3` build hangs at the menu draw. Only the four main-loop
modules (`lw2_math3d`, `lw2_render`, `lw2_flight`, `lw2_gfx_vga`) get `-3`, which
buys real `imul`/`idiv` instead of Watcom's `__I4M`/`__I4D` helper calls.
`tools/build_game.ps1` documents each flag and why it is there.

## Test

```
bash tests/run_unit_tests.sh
```
Expect `UNIT TESTS: all passed`: 12 host tests, 27 oracle gates, 2 source gates.
It takes a few minutes, most of it Unicorn single-stepping 1994 code. The
oracle gates need only gcc and unicorn; the object-hash source gate also needs
Open Watcom, and without it the suite names the missing compiler and fails
rather than under-reporting. `LW2_ALLOW_NO_WATCOM=1` accepts the 40-gate run.

The two source gates are worth knowing about:

- `tools/prove_identical.py` compiles all 20 linked modules and compares each
  against a recorded baseline. Renaming a local or rewriting a comment can't
  move a single instruction, so if a hash moves, the edit did something it
  wasn't supposed to.

  Two things had to be dealt with to make that baseline mean anything off this
  machine, and the second one is a genuine Open Watcom quirk. First, `wcc` stamps
  the source's name into THEADR and every dependency's path and mtime into a
  COMENT class 0xE9 record, so the raw `.obj` hash moves if you merely unzip
  elsewhere or touch a header: the same `lw2_fmt.c` gives a 646-byte object here
  and 661 bytes from a longer path, identical code, 15 bytes of path. The gate
  hashes only the records carrying code and symbols and skips those two. Second,
  and stranger: **Open Watcom's codegen depends on how long the build path is.**
  Compile a byte-identical `lw2_gfx_vga.c` from a 36-character directory and from
  a 39-character one and you get two different functions, with different stack
  slots and an extra reload. It's a threshold, not a slide, and `-oe=80` on that
  module is what exposes it. So the gate doesn't compile where you unzipped: it
  copies `engine/` to one short fixed path and compiles there. The baseline in
  `tools/object_hashes.json` therefore reproduces anywhere, which was tested by
  building it from a 112-character path under a different directory name.
- `tools/check_names.py` fails on a variable named after the register it happened
  to land in during the reverse-engineering. `cl` says where the value sat;
  `shade` says what it is. Deltas (`dx`/`dy`/`dz`), coordinate families
  (`cx`/`cy`/`cz`, `sx`/`sy`) and a `char` called `ch` are exempt, and so are the
  `asm_ref`/`ref_*` models in the tests, whose whole job is to mirror the
  original's registers.

`tools/check_knf.py` checks OpenBSD style(9). It's a standalone tool, not a
gate, and it currently reports about 2,800 long lines: this tree keeps the `@0x`
archaeology in comments, and those comments run past 80 columns. That was a
choice, not an oversight.

## Performance

In DOSBox-X at `cycles=32000`, `game.exe` runs the attract demo at 26.4 fps and
Mission 1 at 46.8, measured with `tools/perf_bench.ps1` against
`tools/perf_baselines.json`. Work per frame fell from 40.3 ms to 25.6 ms across
the optimization pass, a 36% cut (`docs/PROGRESS.md`). The original is faster
still; closing the rest of that gap is open work.

What governs every optimization decision here: in DOSBox-X's normal core, one
emulated cycle is one instruction, flat, and a VGA byte write costs 1 cycle
because `vmemdelay` defaults to 0. The only thing billed at hardware rates is
port I/O, at 16 cycles for a word `OUT` and 25 for a byte. So the currency is
instruction count, not memory traffic, which inverts much of what 1994-era
optimization guides tell you to do. `docs/DOSBOX_COST_MODEL.md` has the
measurements. `docs/PROGRESS.md` records the experiments that came out *slower*
and were reverted, including a parked-index scheme (28.7 to 29.9 ms) and a
RAM-plane render target.

One measurement caveat, in `tools/perf_report.py`: any build that changes frame
timing also changes the autopilot's trajectory, because input is dt-scaled, so
two builds aren't measuring the same scene unless you force it. The work meter
(`-dLW2_DIAG_NOBLIT`) exists to sidestep that.

## The original game files

`reference/original/lw2/` is the 1994 release as shipped. `reference/original/`
also holds the unpacked executable and the extracted driver binaries. The gates
need them: a gate that does not execute the original proves nothing about it.

LineWars II is Copyright 1994 Safari Software and Patrick Aalto, and is a
trademark of Patrick Aalto (`reference/original/lw2/LW2.DOC`). The
reconstruction in `engine/` is a from-scratch C rewrite containing none of the
original's machine code, but it is derived from that work and exists only
because of it. Two headers do carry original *data* rather than code, extracted
verbatim from the binary and regenerable by the scripts in `tools/generators/`:
`lw2_setup_ui.h` (the config-editor UI tables) and the briefing and DS text
tables.

## Status

Feature-complete and play-tested: all ten missions, sound, music, cockpit, HUD,
radar, config screen, F1-F4, pause.

`docs/PROGRESS.md` is the working log rather than a polished document, and open
items live there. The honest summary: this is semantically equivalent per block,
not byte-identical to the original binary. Open Watcom schedules registers
differently than the 1994 compiler did, and byte-identity was dropped early in
favour of portability. Where a gate reports "0 mismatch", it means the compiled C
and the executed original agreed on every input tested, and the test says how
many that was.

## License

The reconstructed C source is Copyright 2026 Fred Angstadt, under the PolyForm
Noncommercial License 1.0.0 (`LICENSE.md`): use it, change it, and share it for
any noncommercial purpose. The original game and its data (`reference/`,
`data/`, `dist/`) remain Copyright 1994 Safari Software and Patrick Aalto and
are redistributed here as freeware with Patrick Aalto's written permission of
July 16, 2026. Commercial use of anything here requires his agreement first.
The DOSBox-X source excerpts in `docs/dbx_src/` are GPL-2.0-or-later and carry
their own license (`docs/dbx_src/COPYING`); none of that code is compiled into
the game. Details in `NOTICE.md`.

# The Bad King — Linux Port

A Linux terminal port of **The Bad King**, a 1991 text-based RPG by Griffin Knodle (Flatrat Production), originally released for Windows 3.x.

Built by decompiling `BADKING.EXE` with Ghidra and fixing the output to compile and run as a native Linux terminal application.

## Building

```
make
```

Requires GCC. Produces the `badking` binary.

## Playing

```
./badking
```

Player name is hardcoded to "thomas". Terminal runs in raw mode (no Enter needed for commands).

**Travel commands:** `m`ove, `l`ook, `t`alk, `s`earch, `c`ast, `a`tatus, `b` save, `q`uit  
**Battle commands:** `f`ight, `c`ast, `r`un

## How It Works

The original `BADKING.EXE` is a 16-bit NE (New Executable) for Windows 3.x, compiled with Borland C++. Ghidra decompiled it to C, but the output had ~40 compilation errors, missing string data, and DOS/Windows system calls that don't exist on Linux.

The port fixes this by:

1. **Embedding string data** — 292 game strings extracted from the binary's data segment into `strings.c`
2. **Embedding the data segment** — the full 20KB data segment (navigation tables, character classification, item data) extracted into `dataseg.c`
3. **Replacing DOS/Windows I/O** — `swi(0x21)` interrupt stubs and Windows API calls replaced with standard C (`printf`, `getchar`, `fopen`, `fscanf`, `fprintf`, `time`, `exit`)
4. **Fixing 16-bit→64-bit issues** — data segment offsets converted to proper pointers via `DS()` macro, 16-bit table reads fixed, function signatures corrected
5. **Terminal raw mode** — `termios` for character-at-a-time input matching the original Windows message loop behavior

## Files

| File | Description |
|---|---|
| `decompiled.c` | Main game code — Ghidra decompilation with all Linux fixes applied |
| `strings.c` | 292 game string literals extracted from the binary (auto-generated) |
| `dataseg.c` | Full data segment from `BADKING.EXE` embedded as a C array (auto-generated) |
| `compat.h` | Type definitions (`undefined1`, `undefined2`, etc.), calling convention stubs, Ghidra helper macros |
| `decls.h` | Global variable declarations (game state, data segment references) |
| `dataseg.h` | Macros for data segment access (`DS()`, `DS_MUT()`, buffer names) |
| `decompiled_strings.txt` | Reference file mapping string offsets to their text content |
| `BADKING.EXE` | Original 16-bit Windows 3.x binary (NE format, 67KB) |
| `Makefile` | Build: `gcc -Wno-all decompiled.c strings.c dataseg.c -o badking` |

## Known Limitations

- Player name is hardcoded to "thomas" (original line input was replaced)
- Windows GUI functions (scrolling, caret, painting) are stubs — the game was always text-mode through an EasyWin window
- Some C runtime internals (locale, timezone parsing) are stubbed out
- 23 `swi(0x21)` DOS interrupt stubs remain in dead code paths (Windows init, C runtime internals) — none are reachable from the game

kq6up-ice051-source-readme-md.text:
# ICE 0.51 — recovered source

GitHub baseline: [contents, macOS run instructions, and reverting changes](docs/BASELINE.md).
The original Mac executable is preserved under `snapshots/macos-arm64/ice`.
The current build fixes macOS terminal characters and locates its data automatically; see [native runtime notes](docs/NATIVE_RUNTIME.md).


Fortran source for the U.S. Naval Observatory's **Interactive Computer
Ephemeris, version 0.51** (Nautical Almanac Office, 1988–89), recovered from
`ICE.EXE` (Microsoft FORTRAN 4.x, DOS, EXEPACK-compressed, 8087 emulator).

No original source was available. Everything here was rebuilt from the
machine code. The program's logic, constants, order of evaluation, I/O
statements and FORMATs follow the binary routine by routine. Each routine's
header gives its address in the executable, e.g. `RISSET [0A09:0000]`. The
names of routines and variables are mine.

All 74 routines of the program are recovered, which is everything in the
executable except the Microsoft FORTRAN run-time library. That covers the
menu, all ten function keys, the NOVAS astrometry, the Chebyshev ephemeris
reader, the physical ephemeris, the catalogs and the five assembler helpers.

## Files

| file | contents |
|---|---|
| `src/ice.for` | main program, menu, `ICE.DFT` defaults, F2 file output (`ICE MENU DFTMSG BADCHR HITKEY FILOUT`) |
| `src/inival.for` | F1 Initial Values (`INIVAL`) |
| `src/positn.for` | F3 Positions: apparent, astrometric, heliocentric, barycentric, Chebyshev listing (`POSITN POLYLS`) |
| `src/physui.for` | F4 Physical Ephemeris screen (`PHYSIC`) |
| `src/sidtbl.for` | F5 Sidereal Time (`SIDTBL`) |
| `src/risset.for` | F6 Rise, Transit, Set and twilight (`RISSET`) |
| `src/navig.for` | F7 Navigation (`NAVIG`) |
| `src/daycon.for` | F8 Daily Configuration (`DAYCON`) |
| `src/catalog.for` | F9 Change Catalog, object lookup, angle editing (`CATCHG NXTCAT LOOKUP DMSTR LATLON GETNAM`) |
| `src/catdata.for` | built-in catalog: the first 200 FK5 stars as loaded at start-up (generated by `tools_catdata.py`) |
| `src/novas1.for` | NOVAS: places, precession, nutation (IAU 1980, `nod_data.inc`), aberration, light deflection, sidereal time, refraction (`PLACE APSTAR APPLAN ASSTAR ASPLAN SIDTIM NOD …`) |
| `src/ephem.for` | the DE200-based Chebyshev ephemeris: `PARAM.DAT`, `EPHnn.DAT`, bit-packed coefficients (`SOLSYS PARAMS EPHRD LOCATE COEFS CHEBEV UNPACK CHEB CHEBD`) |
| `src/physic.for` | physical ephemeris of the planets and Moon, vector utilities (`PHYSEP ROTEL PMAG FRAME PROJ PLCOOR DOT …`) |
| `src/util.for` | angle/time editing, date input and output, character utilities (`ANGSTR DATJD CALDAT NBLANK MATCH UPCASE IVAL DAYSYM`) |
| `src/deltat.for` | ΔT, the original 1988 polynomials (`DELTAT`) |
| `src/alt/deltat26.for` | ΔT replacement: observed values to 2026, extrapolated to 2050 (the same routine as in `ICE_DT26.EXE`) |
| `src/catlg.inc` | `COMMON /CATLG/ /CATNAM/`: the catalog page in memory |
| `src/scrio.asm` | the original assembler helpers `SETCUR GETKEY CLRWIN CUROFF CURON DOSXIT` (MASM) |
| `src/scrio.c` | stand-ins for the helpers when building with gfortran, plus MS console behaviour (see below) |
| `dos/` | the same sources in code page 437 with CR LF line ends and `$INCLUDE`, for Microsoft FORTRAN 4.x |
| `build.sh` | gfortran build |
| `setup_data.py` | prepares a data directory for the gfortran build from the original ICE files |
| `tools_cp437.py`, `tools_catdata.py` | build helpers |
| `verify/` | the screen-by-screen comparison against the original program |

The `.for` files in `src/` are UTF-8, so the box-drawing characters can be
read and edited. The build converts them to code page 437, which is what the
program writes.

## Getting started: Linux, macOS, and DOS

Install the prerequisites listed for your platform below, then clone the repository:

```sh
git clone https://github.com/kq6up/ice051-source.git
cd ice051-source
```

### Linux (native GNU Fortran build)

You need GNU Fortran (`gfortran`), a C compiler available as `gcc`, and
Python 3. For Debian/Ubuntu, install them with:

```sh
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git build-essential gfortran python3
```

Other distributions can install equivalent packages through their package
manager; see the [Fortran installation guide](https://fortran-lang.org/learn/os_setup/install_gfortran/).
From the repository directory:

```sh
./build.sh                    # build/ice: vintage Delta T model
./run.sh
```

For the updated model, build and run its separate executable:

```sh
./build.sh --deltat2026        # build/ice-dt2026
./run.sh --deltat2026
```

The tracked `data/` directory is already converted for GNU Fortran. No data
conversion is needed for a normal checkout. The user has also tested the
Linux version successfully on **Slackware ARM64 (aarch64)** and reports that
it works well. The native macOS build and launchers have been tested here.

### macOS (native GNU Fortran build)

Install Apple's command-line tools and GNU Fortran. With
[Homebrew](https://brew.sh/) already installed:

```sh
xcode-select --install        # only if the command-line tools are absent
brew install gcc python      # GNU Fortran is included in the gcc formula
./build.sh
./run.sh
```

After building, you can also double-click **Start ICE.command** in Finder.
That launcher selects the vintage model. To select the updated model:

```sh
./build.sh --deltat2026
./run.sh --deltat2026
```

The [Homebrew gcc formula](https://formulae.brew.sh/formula/gcc) supplies
`gfortran`; Apple's `gcc` command supplies the C compiler used by the script.
The macOS build creates `build/libiceconsole.dylib` for terminal character
conversion. Keep it beside an executable if you relocate that executable.
Rebuild on a different computer to link against its installed runtime libraries.

### DOS (historical or rebuilt executable)

Install [DOSBox-X](https://dosbox-x.com/) with `dosbox-x` available on PATH,
and Python 3 for the host-side launcher. From the repository:

```sh
python3 dosbox/prepare.py
python3 dosbox/lab.py launch                 # rebuilt vintage model
python3 dosbox/lab.py launch --deltat2026     # updated 2026 Delta T model
python3 dosbox/lab.py launch --original      # supplied historical executable
```

Preparation creates a local `dosbox/drive_c/` with separate program directories
and the original DOS data. It refuses to overwrite an existing drive.
The prebuilt DOS executables need no compiler. To rebuild them with Microsoft
FORTRAN 4.10 and MASM 5.10, follow [the DOS workflow](dosbox/README.md).
The Microsoft compiler distribution is not included in this Git repository.

In the separate complete DOS lab ZIP, double-click **Start DOS ICE.command**,
**Start DOS ICE 2026.command**, or **Start Historical DOS ICE.command**.
Keep the extracted lab folder together. Its launchers locate their files from
any working directory.

On a real DOS system, extract `reference/ice.zip` into a directory. For a
rebuilt version, replace that directory's `ICE.EXE` with either
`dosbox/bin/ice-vintage.exe` or `dosbox/bin/ice-dt2026.exe`, naming it `ICE.EXE`.
Run it with that directory as the current DOS directory so it finds its data.
The live rebuild and Sun checks used DOSBox-X on Apple Silicon macOS; real
DOS hardware has not been tested here.

### Keys, data, and model selection

Use F1 for initial values, F7 for celestial navigation, and F10 to quit.
On a Mac keyboard you may need Fn with the function key. Inside DOSBox-X,
type `EXIT` after F10 to close the remaining DOS prompt. Alt-F1 redraws the
menu. Native terminal output uses UTF-8; `ICE_CP437=1` selects raw DOS bytes.
Output files keep the original CP437 encoding.

Native `run.sh` can be invoked by absolute path from any working directory.
It finds the converted data automatically; set `ICE_DATA_DIR` to select a
specific data folder. Relative output files are written in the directory
from which you launch the program. See [native runtime notes](docs/NATIVE_RUNTIME.md).

Keep the native and DOS data formats separate. `PARAM.DAT` and `EPHnn.DAT`
in the original DOS package use Microsoft Fortran record framing. If you need
to prepare another native data folder, first extract the original DOS package
into a separate directory, then run:

```sh
python3 setup_data.py /path/to/original-dos-data /path/to/new-native-data
```

Do not pass the already converted native `data/` as this script's input.
The catalogs are copied unchanged.

Both platforms' updated builds select the existing 2026 Delta T replacement
and change F7's decimal-year day divisor from 30 to 365.25. Other documented
historical bugs remain; further fixes are deferred. The DOS workflow leaves
the Linux and macOS build files unchanged.

## Editing your local initial values: ICE.DFT

**Yes: `ICE.DFT` is a hand-editable plain-text file.** ICE reads it at startup.
Changes accepted on the F1 screen last for the current session; they are not
saved back to this file. Edit the file with ICE closed, save it as plain text,
and restart to load your defaults.

Edit the copy associated with the program you run:

| Program | Defaults file |
|---|---|
| Native Linux/macOS | `data/ICE.DFT`, or `ICE.DFT` in your selected `ICE_DATA_DIR` |
| Prepared DOS vintage build | `dosbox/drive_c/ICE/ICE.DFT` |
| Prepared DOS 2026 build | `dosbox/drive_c/ICE26/ICE.DFT` |
| Prepared historical DOS reference | `dosbox/drive_c/ORIGINAL/ICE.DFT` |
| Extracted DOS lab ZIP | The corresponding `drive_c/ICE/`, `drive_c/ICE26/`, or `drive_c/ORIGINAL/` copy |

The six lines have this order. Columns are counted from 1:

| Line | Value | Numeric field | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Starting date/time | Columns 18-32 | `YYYYMMDD.HHMMSS`, e.g. `20261013.230000` |
| 2 | Latitude | Columns 18-32 | Decimal degrees: north positive, south negative |
| 3 | Longitude | Columns 18-32 | Decimal degrees: east positive, west negative |
| 4 | Tabulation interval | Columns 18-32 | `1.000000` means one day; calendar-style intervals are also accepted |
| 5 | Number of positions/lines | Columns 24-26 | Integer count for tables |
| 6 | Time zone | Columns 24-26 | Integer offset: local time minus UTC, in hours |

For example, this starts at 34 N, 117 W, with a UTC-7 time-zone setting.
These are illustrative values from the Sun test, not a change to your files:

```text
Starting date =  20261013.230000
Latitude      =        34.000000
Longitude     =      -117.000000
Time step     =         1.000000
Num. of positions =      1
Time zone     =         -7
```

Preserve the leading spaces and alignment; replace only the numeric values.
Use spaces rather than tabs, decimal points rather than commas, and no degree
symbols or N/S/E/W suffixes. Convert minutes to decimal degrees: 34 degrees
30 minutes N is `34.500000`. The text labels before the numeric fields are
ignored by the reader. Do not append comments inside the numeric fields.

The time-zone value is a fixed offset: use `-7` for UTC-7 or `-8` for UTC-8.
ICE does not change it automatically for daylight saving time.
**F7 navigation uses UTC and ignores this zone offset.** Enter a UTC date/time
for a Sun shot even if line 6 contains your local zone. The zone setting is
used for F6 rise/set times; other tables label their own time scales.
The startup date is fixed until you edit it or change it through F1; it does
not automatically follow the computer clock.

### Keep personal settings out of Git

The native `data/ICE.DFT` is tracked, so editing it makes a local Git change.
For personal defaults without modifying tracked files, copy the native data
folder outside the checkout and select that copy:

```sh
cp -R data ../ice-local-data
# Hand-edit ../ice-local-data/ICE.DFT in a plain-text editor.
ICE_DATA_DIR="$(pwd)/../ice-local-data" ./run.sh --deltat2026
```

Use an absolute `ICE_DATA_DIR` path when launching from elsewhere. The prepared
DOS `dosbox/drive_c/` is already ignored by Git, and the extracted DOS lab is
separate from the checkout. You can hand-edit those defaults locally without
committing them. Data preparation may replace defaults when recreating a
folder, so keep a copy of your personalized `ICE.DFT` before rebuilding a drive
or rerunning data conversion. Compiling the native program alone leaves the
defaults file intact.

## How it was checked

* **Routine level:** 35 routines were called inside the original
  executable (under a CPU emulator) and in the recovered source with the same
  random arguments: 60–400 cases each, including stateful sequences for the
  ephemeris reader. Character and integer routines, the coefficient unpacking,
  the ephemeris reader and the date routines agree exactly. Floating-point
  results agree to 1e-16–1e-11 relative. The few larger differences
  (nutation 1e-7, which is single precision in the original; refraction;
  sidereal time near 1e9 s) come from x87 register use, explained below.
* **Program level** (`verify/`): 86 scripted sessions covering every
  function key, error paths, both catalogs and file output. Each one is run
  through the original `ICE.EXE` (unpacked, under a small DOS emulator) and
  through the gfortran build. The final 80×25 screen, the complete stream of
  screen output and every file written are compared. All 86 agree, except
  for two known run-time differences, which are listed below: the last digit
  of some Chebyshev coefficients, and a file opened on two units.

```sh
pip install unicorn capstone numpy
verify/run.sh /path/to/ice            # all 86 sessions
verify/run.sh /path/to/ice F6         # only those whose name contains "F6"
```

`verify/prepare.py` unpacks `ICE.EXE` and checks it against the version used
here (ICE 0.51, 152 KB EXE).

## Known differences (run-time library, not the source)

* MS FORTRAN never prints the optional leading zero in F, E and D output
  (`  .7174172`, ` -.0474`), and gfortran always does (`0.7174172`). The
  comparison maps both to the MS form.
* MS FORTRAN keeps intermediate results in 80-bit registers across
  statements, while gfortran `-O0` stores them as doubles. This changes the
  last digit of a few of the 15-digit Chebyshev coefficients in the F3/F5
  listing (Moon, Mars, Jupiter; the Sun's are identical). Elsewhere the
  effect stays far below anything displayed.
* The MS run-time refuses to open a file that is already open on another
  unit, and gfortran allows it. This shows only if `ICE.DFT`, which the
  original never closes, is given to F9 as a catalog.
* `scrio.c` reproduces the console behaviour of the MS run-time, which
  gfortran lacks: carriage control, `PAUSE`, and a READ ending the pending
  output line.

The verification also turned up an emulator problem: QEMU/Unicorn computes
the x87 transcendental instructions in double precision, so the original
under emulation printed `10**3` as 1000.0000000000013. `verify/x87fix.py`
restores 80-bit results, which were checked against a real x87.

## Quirks of the original, kept as they are

* F7 Navigation forms the year as IY + IM/12 + **ID/30**, so ΔT is taken up
  to two years late in December. `--deltat2026` corrects this.
* If `ICE.DFT` is missing, the "built-in defaults" are replaced by zeros
  (`MENU`).
* `SOLSYS` can refresh the Sun and Moon from a stale buffer when the body's
  interval is still valid.
* F3/F5 writes the Chebyshev listing to unit 11, which is the catalog unit,
  and then closes it. If a catalog file is open, the listing goes into it.
* F6 tests `NUM .EQ. 0` where the Sun (10) was surely meant. As a result,
  evening twilight stays blank on days the Sun does not rise.
* F6 has `ANGSTR` write 10 characters into `CHARACTER*6 STRT(2)`, which
  relies on the two elements being adjacent. The astrometric-places file
  header is in column 28, while the screen header is in column 26.
* `LATLON` normalises the longitude in place, which changes `ALONG` in
  `/SITE/`. `CLRWIN` returns with `RET 8` for 16 bytes of arguments, but it
  is never called.

anpage-remech2-rs-readme-md.text:
ReMech2 is an **unofficial** open-source reimplementation of the game _MechWarrior 2: 31st Century Combat_, built for modern operating systems. This is still a work-in-progress and things are rough and hacky, but the game currently works well enough to play on Windows 11 or Linux. > [!IMPORTANT] > **This project does not include the original game data at all.** You must supply your own copy of the game to run it. See [Running](#running).

## Features - A new installer that runs before the sim - Checks the game's files and music - Can install the game from CD-ROM, .ISO or .BIN/.CUE image, or folder - Improved mouse input - Advanced support for joysticks and other devices (HOTAS/HOSAS) - An internal MIDI synthesizer and soundfont - Music playback from files instead of CD audio - Optional automatic ripping of CD audio to FLAC - Wgpu-based, aspect-correct drawing and upscaling (Vulkan/DirectX/OpenGL) - 16:9 Hor+ widescreen support - Unlocked framerates (up to 181 FPS, experimental) And more... ## Bug Fixes - Jump jet fuel now recharges regardless of framerate - Missiles no longer explode in your face at high framerates - Your mech's heat no longer creeps higher when the game is paused - It is no longer impossible to explode from overheating - The background music no longer restarts when the game is paused There is more to come as work progresses. ## Running You'll need a copy of the **English** version of the original game. See [Supported Versions](#supported-versions) below. This can either be a real CD or your own backup in .ISO or .BIN/.CUE format. ### Game Not Installed If you don't currently have the game installed, simply run ReMech2. You will be prompted to install the necessary data from CD, a disc image, or a folder. The game data will be installed to one of these locations, depending on system settings: - Windows: `%LOCALAPPDATA%\ReMech2\data\game` - Linux: `~/.local/share/remech2/game` If installing from a source that includes CD audio, the music will be automatically ripped to the correct location as FLAC files. See [Music](#music) below. #### Portable Mode If you want ReMech2 to install the game files into the game's working directory, create a file called `portable.txt`. All game data, configuration files, save files, and logs will be written to this folder. ### Game Already Installed If you do currently have an installed copy of the game, ReMech2 can be dropped into the same folder as `MW2.PRJ`. It will run in portable mode in this case as well. ### Supported Versions Any disc with the software-rendered release, either for DOS or Windows 95: - IBM CD-ROM - Pentium Edition - Windows 95/MS-DOS - SideWinder 3D Pro - SoftKey > [!NOTE] > Some later releases of the Windows and DOS combo discs have a few duplicated music tracks that overwrite the intended songs. > ReMech2 has no way to account for this, so ideally you'll want to use the MS-DOS-only, "Pentium Edition," or SideWinder 3D Pro discs. > [!CAUTION] > The SoftKey release lacks CD audio completely. > If that's what you have, you'll need to go without in-game music or source the tracks from elsewhere. ### Not Supported - S3 ViRGE - Matrox Mystique - ATI 3D RAGE / RAGE II - 3Dfx Voodoo/Diamond Monster 3D/STB Velocity - PowerVR - Battlepack - Titanium Ghost Bear's Legacy and Mercenaries are also **not supported**. ### Music > [!IMPORTANT] > The original game played its background music from the Red Book audio on the CD. > **ReMech2 plays the game's background music from files instead.** Put the tracks in a `Music` folder in the game data directory (next to `MW2.PRJ`), named `track02` through `track27`, case insensitive. If any tracks are missing, ReMech2 will prompt you to rip them, or you can open the configured music folder from a button in the UI. > [!NOTE] > **WAV**, **OGG**, **MP3**, and **FLAC** files are supported. The numbering matches the CD's original track numbers, which is why it starts at 2. Track 1 on the disc is always game data. If the folder is missing or contains no files matching that pattern, the game has no music. The folder can be changed in the `remech2.toml` that is created the first time the game is run. ```toml [audio] music_path="Music" ``` `music_path` can either be relative to the game data directory or an absolute path. ## Building ### Requirements - [The Rust toolchain](https://rustup.rs/) - A C/C++ compiler - `libclang` #### Linux - `clang` - `mold` (by default) - `libasound2-dev` - `libudev-dev` #### Windows MSVC isn't currently supported. - MinGW-w64 - `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` - `rustup target add x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` ### Steps Nothing special for a Rust project. ![](decal.png)

# First Byte's ProVoice (Reborn)

ProVoice covers these classic synthesizers created by First Byte in the 80s and 90s:

- **Smooth Talker** (includes the v2 and Dr Sbaitso voices)
- **Monologue** (includes all known voices, 16-bit voices converted to 32-bit for the
  first time ever. well known for being using in devices like the DoubleTalk)

First Byte's ProVoice 2.12 speech engine (`FBVTV32.DLL`, June 1997: the text-to-speech
behind Monologue for Windows), decompiled to C and rebuilt. Two changes from the
original:

- **No registry.** Voices are read from a `Voices` folder next to the DLL, so nothing
  needs installing and no admin rights are needed.
- **More voices.** Tools in `tools/` convert the 16-bit Monologue voices, and the
  DOS voices of Dr. Sbaitso and SmoothTalker 2.2, into 32-bit ProVoice voices.

Otherwise the engine behaves exactly like the original: same 39 exports, same output.
The one addition, an adjustable sentence pause, is off by default.
Its test suite checks the recompiled DLL against the original byte for byte (every
voice, phonetic command, dictionary operation, playback and the settings dialogs).

For programming against the DLL, see **[API.md](API.md)**.

## How it works

1. **Text → phonetics** (`src/rulepass.c`, `rules.c`, `textedit.c`, `dict.c`,
   `intonation.c`). Each voice carries its own rule programs (RULE resources). They
   split text into sentences, expand numbers and abbreviations, and apply
   letter-to-sound rules, after looking words up in the dictionaries. An intonation
   pass then adds stress, pitch and timing commands.
2. **Phonetics → audio** (`src/synth.c`, `render.c`, `phon.c`, `backend.c`). The
   synthesizer strings together the voice's recorded speech units and bends each
   waveform period to the target pitch and speed. It also emits sync events: mouth
   shapes, words and bookmarks.
3. **Playback** (`src/output.c`, `playback.c`). A thread streams the audio through
   `waveOut`, and an event thread posts each sync event to the application at the
   moment it is heard.
4. **Voices** (`src/fontload.c`, `voices.c`). A voice is a resource-only DLL: phoneme
   set, rules, recordings and prosody values, with an optional `.INI` for its default
   dictionary and description.

## Layout

| Path                       | Contents                                                                                   |
| -------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `src/`, `include/`         | The engine in C                                                                            |
| `standalone/`              | Export table (`.def`), resources (`.rc`), global variables; generated                      |
| `test/`                    | Test programs: `fbvtest` (engine), `playtest` (playback and dialogs), `speak`, `voicetest` |
| `tools/`                   | Voice/dictionary converters and the decompilation tools                                    |
| `test32/`                  | Scripts for testing against the original engine                                            |
| `names.txt`, `globals.txt` | Every function and global of the original, with its address                                |
| `patents/`                 | First Byte's speech patents                                                                |

## Building

Requires a 32-bit (i686) MinGW-w64 toolchain, such as [WinLibs](https://winlibs.com).
The engine is x86-only and uses GCC inline assembly, so MSVC won't build it.

```sh
cmake -S . -B cmake-build -G Ninja
cmake --build cmake-build
```

This produces `cmake-build/FBVTV32.DLL` and the test programs. To use the DLL, put a
`Voices` folder next to it (see [API.md](API.md#setup)), then try it:

```sh
cmake-build/speak.exe ESNB1K8 "Hello, world."
cmake-build/speak.exe -o hello.wav ESNB1K8 "Hello, world."
```

`speak` uses the `FBVTV32.DLL` in its own folder. `-o` saves a WAV file instead of
playing, and `-p ms` sets the pause after each sentence (default 500; `-1` = the
original engine's pauses, see [API.md](API.md#parameters)).

## Verifying against the original

`build.sh` builds the engine and compares it with the original DLL. It needs files
that are not in this repository: the original `Fbvtv32.dll` and the voices, from
Monologue for Win32.

1. `python tools/fbvpatch.py ORIGINAL/Fbvtv32.dll test32/Fbvtv32.dll` — a copy of
   the original that works without admin rights.
2. Put the 32-bit voices and dictionaries in `test32/Voice32/`.
3. `python test32/make_reg.py` (reads `Monologue 32-bit/speech_fonts_install_64bit.reg`),
   then import `test32/provoice_test_install.reg` (admin). The original engine finds
   its voices in the registry.
4. `sh build.sh` (set `BIN` in it to your toolchain's `bin`). It prints `IDENTICAL` for both test suites, then copies the DLL to
   `dist/`. Add `--quick` for a shorter run; `sh coverage.sh` shows which code the
   tests exercise.

`python tools/fbvgen.py` checks `names.txt` against the `// @address` markers in
`src/`. `tools/fbvsa.py` regenerates `standalone/` from the original DLL (the CMake
target `regen`).

## Converting voices

| Tool                                          | Converts                                                                                 |
| --------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `tools/fbvconv.py SRC.DLL DST.DLL`            | 16-bit Monologue voice → 32-bit                                                          |
| `tools/dicconv.py SRC.DIC DST.DIC`            | 16-bit dictionary → 32-bit                                                               |
| `tools/dosport.py VOICE DST.DLL DONOR.DLL`    | DOS voice (`sbaitso`, `st22male`, `st22female`) → 32-bit, using a ProVoice voice's rules |
| `tools/mkvoices.py SRC DEST [--reg FILE.reg]` | Voice directory → `Voices` folder with `.INI` settings                                   |

## Building a voice from recordings

`tools/fbvbuild.py` makes a new speech font from a phone-aligned corpus in
the CMU ARCTIC layout (`wav/<id>.wav`, `.txt`, `.TextGrid`):

```sh
python tools/fbvbuild.py C:/path/to/cmu_us_bdl_arctic
python tools/fbvbuild.py C:/path/to/cmu_us_bdl_arctic --rate 11025 --bits 8
```

The front-end (letter-to-sound rules, dictionaries, prosody) comes from a
donor font (`--donor`, default ESNA2K6). The demi-diphone units are cut from
the recordings: each transcript runs through the donor's own rules
(`speak -t`), is aligned to the TextGrid, and is cut at ZFF pitch marks
(`tools/get_pitchmarks.py`). The result, with a copy of the engine to try it,
goes to `build/voicebuild/<NAME>/`; `report.txt` there lists coverage, check
results and the units to listen to first. Copy `Voices/<NAME>.DLL` and
`.INI` into `dist/Voices` yourself once you like it.

The front-end phonetics and pitch marks are cached in
`build/voicebuild/cache/<SPEAKER>/`, tied to the corpus path, transcripts and
wav sizes and dates, so a second run is much faster. Utterances whose
phonetics use a symbol the font lacks are dropped; `report.txt` says which.

# Wings of Fury for the Atari STE

Brøderbund's Wings of Fury was never released for the Atari ST. This is a conversion of the Amiga version (1990)
for the Atari STE and Mega STE: all 15 maps, the ranks, the forward view, saved games, the original samples and
music.

![Take-off](docs/img/takeoff.png) ![Enemy fighters over an island](docs/img/zeros.png)

It is a re-implementation, not a recompile. The Amiga program was taken apart to learn exactly how the game
behaves, and that behaviour was written again in C++ on top of [AGT](https://bitbucket.org/d_m_l/agtools), dml's
Atari Game Tools. The graphics, maps, samples and music are converted from the Amiga files by scripts.

| | |
|---|---|
| Machine | Atari STE or Mega STE, 2 MB of memory or more |
| Display | colour monitor or TV, 50 Hz |
| Controls | joystick in port 1 (on the deck also cursor keys and space) |
| Media | one 720 KB floppy, or a folder on a hard disk |

Ready-made disk image and hard disk version: [atari.love/wof](https://atari.love/wof/). The player's manual is
[manual/README.TXT](manual/README.TXT).

## What differs from the Amiga

- 16 colours on screen instead of 32; the pictures are reduced to fit.
- The sound plays through the STE's DMA sample hardware at 12.5 kHz, mixed in software.
- The briefing, name entry and hall of fame are in low resolution.
- Added: a pause page, a help page (H), a loading screen, Ctrl+Q to quit.
- Left out: the demo mode.

The remaining differences and open points are listed in [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md).

## The repository

**`game/`** is the game itself. Nearly all of it is one file, `wof.cpp` (7400 lines): flight model, enemies,
weapons, missions, the front end, saved games and all drawing that AGT does not do. Beside it are the DMA sound
mixer (`snd.h`), the player for the original's menu music (`music.h`), the tables the tools generate
(`flight_data.h`, `snd_data.h` and others), the `Makefile`, and `assets_com.sh`, which cuts the graphics with AGT's
cutter. `game/source_assets/` holds what the cutter reads: per map a level picture and its map data, and the
sprite sheets (Hellcat, enemy planes, effects, crew, weapons, panel, fonts), all already in the port's 16 colours.

**`tools/`** is everything that runs on the development machine, in Python and shell:
- the decoders for the Amiga formats (`rpck.py`, `ppkc.py`, `iff.py`, `hunk.py`) and `convert_gfx.py`, which
  writes every picture and sprite frame out as PNG;
- the converters that turn those into the port's assets: `make_proto_assets.py` (levels, maps, sprite sheets, the
  colour reduction from 32 to 16), `make_panel.py`, `make_pics.py`, `make_sounds.py`, `make_music.py`,
  `make_intro.py`, the two font builders; `regen_assets.sh` runs them all;
- the release builders: `pack_disk.py` (ZX0 packing and the file bundles for the floppy), `make_st.py` (writes
  the 720 KB disk image), `make_release.sh`;
- the test rig: `run_hatari.sh`, `hatari_play.py` (plays one recorded flight in Hatari and collects screenshots),
  `suite.sh` (a set of them), `snapdiff.py` (compares the screenshots of two runs);
- `env.sh`, where all of them find AGT, the compiler, Python and Hatari.

**`tests/`** holds 51 recorded flights. Each is a text file of joystick input per game tick, with points where a
screenshot is taken and, in many, the result that must come out (the sequence of player states, the score). They
cover take-off and landing, each weapon, each kind of crash, the enemies, sinking ships, the front end and saved
games.

**`agt-patch/`** is one file, `agtools-local.patch`: the changes to AGT that the game needs, as a diff against
AGT's `master`. [docs/AGT_CHANGES.md](docs/AGT_CHANGES.md) explains each one.

**`amiga-original/`** holds the game's own files as they are on the Amiga disk: the program `wings`, the 15 maps, the
packed sprite banks and pictures in `shapes/`, the samples in `sounds/`, the songs and their player, the font.
Everything else is derived from these.

**`amiga-graphics/`** is the Amiga graphics decoded for inspection: each full-screen picture, a contact sheet per sprite
bank, every single frame under `frames/<bank>/` with its hot spot in `_frames.json`, the palettes, and a rendered
preview of each map in `maps/`. The converters read the frames from here.

**`reverse-engineering/`** is the reverse engineering of the Amiga program: the flat image `wings.bin`, the disassembly
(`wings_raw.s`), the Ghidra decompilation of all 743 functions (`wings_decomp.c`, and `wings_named.c` with names
applied), the call graph, the names found so far (`names/`) and the Ghidra scripts. `reverse-engineering/notes/` is the part to
read: one document per subsystem (player and flight, enemies, weapons and missions, rendering and sound, front
end, forward view, music) with the constants, tables, state machines and timings the port was written from, plus
`DESIGN.md`, the plan of the port, and `sound_ste.md`, the sound on the STE.

**`manual/`** holds `README.TXT`, the player's manual that goes on the disk (38 columns, so that it reads on an ST
in low resolution).

**`docs/`** holds the documents listed below, the screenshots of this page, and `sidecartridge/`: the report of a
file seek fault in the SidecarTridge cartridge's drive emulation, with a test program.

## Documents

- [docs/BUILDING.md](docs/BUILDING.md): what is needed, how to build, test and make a release
- [docs/AGT_CHANGES.md](docs/AGT_CHANGES.md): each change to AGT and why it was needed (the split screen on
  the standard display, the 200 Hz clock, level memory, file access)
- [docs/FORMATS.md](docs/FORMATS.md): the Amiga version's file formats
- [reverse-engineering/notes/](reverse-engineering/notes/): how the original works, subsystem by subsystem; `DESIGN.md` is the plan of the port,
  `sound_ste.md` the sound on the STE
- [docs/sidecartridge/](docs/sidecartridge/): a file seek fault of the SidecarTridge cartridge's drive emulation,
  with a test program
- [BACKLOG.md](BACKLOG.md): open points

## Building, in short

    git clone https://bitbucket.org/d_m_l/agtools.git ../agtools
    (cd ../agtools && git checkout a155d41 && git apply --whitespace=nowarn ../wings-of-fury-atari-ste/agt-patch/agtools-local.patch)
    python3 -m venv .venv && .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements.txt
    cd game && make                      # needs the m68k-atari-mint cross compiler
    cd .. && tools/make_release.sh        # floppy image and hard disk version in builds/

Details are in [docs/BUILDING.md](docs/BUILDING.md).

## How it works

- The game logic runs at the original's 12.5 ticks per second and draws every third vertical blank (16.7 frames
  per second), which is the Amiga version's own rate.
- The playfield is an AGT tile playfield, 16x16 tiles, scrolled by the STE's hardware; the larger maps are over 1500
  tiles (25000 pixels) wide. Below it, split off by a raster colour change, is the cockpit panel in its own palette.
- Sprites are drawn with the blitter. Large or rarely drawn sheets use AGT's plain sprite format, small frequent
  ones its compiled format, because the compiled sheets cost their file size in memory.
- Waves, sinking ships and damage to buildings are changes to the tile map: the game keeps its own tile blocks for
  them and marks the changed cells for redraw.
- The forward view in the panel's centre window is drawn by the game straight into the screen buffer.
- Sound: four voices mixed in software into a DMA buffer.
- One map is in memory at a time, in a zone that is emptied as a whole. On the floppy the data is packed with ZX0
  and unpacked on load.
- Testing: flights recorded as scripts are replayed in Hatari; where behaviour was in doubt, the same situation
  was set up in the Amiga version in vAmiga and compared.

## Credits and rights

Wings of Fury was written by Steve Waldo and published by Brøderbund Software. AGT is the work of dml.

The code of this conversion was written by Claude (Anthropic) in Claude Code, directed and tested on real
machines by the repository's owner.

The conversion's own code, tools, tests and documents are under the MIT licence; [NOTICE](NOTICE) says exactly
what [the licence](LICENSE) covers.

Wings of Fury is copyright 1987, 1990 Brøderbund Software, Inc. This is an unofficial fan conversion, free of
charge. The graphics, maps and sound are taken from the Amiga original and are included here so that the game can
be built, as are the disassembly and decompilation of the Amiga program; they remain the property of their owners
and the MIT licence does not apply to them. Nor does it apply to the AGT patch, which is a diff of dml's code.
